title: Name the Question
subtitle: Every hard question is one of a few kinds. Hear which kind it is, and you know how to think about it — and what to say.
intro: Experienced people do something before they speak that you rarely see: they recognise the kind of question they have been asked. Should we…? is not the same question as Why…?, and each has a way of thinking that works.

steps.d: Find its circle on the map. Beware of look-alikes.
Run that kind’s lens. It leads to a short list of answers.
Point, reason, stop. Then hold it under pushback.

branches.asked: You are being asked whether to commit — when you cannot be sure how it will turn out.
branches.breaks: When there is no time to test, a pilot is just a delay. That is when the fast tools matter more.

leaves.name: Plan–Do–Check–Act
leaves.desc: when you can test it first

leaves.name: The OODA Loop
leaves.desc: when there is no time to test

leaves.name: Intel Foundry Gamble
leaves.desc: a bet, or a sunk-cost trap?

leaves.name: The Hiring Tool
leaves.desc: fast, but can you explain it?

lens.g: If not, the bar for acting rises.

lens.q: Can we try it small first?
lens.g: A test only helps if it can show us something we do not already know.
If waiting is cheap, there is no hurry. If the cost keeps growing, there is no time for a test.

leads.d: It can be undone, it can be tested, and waiting is cheap.
Hard to undo, but it can be done in steps, with a checkpoint between them.
Waiting costs more than a wrong move, or there is nothing to test.
It cannot be undone or tested, and the case is not strong enough.

example.q: Should we move the whole company to a four-day week?
run: Undo it? Mostly. It can be reversed, though staff will not enjoy losing it.
Try it small? Yes: one or two teams, for a fixed period, with the measures agreed in advance.
Cost of waiting? A little in recruitment, not much else.
So: a pilot.
example.say: I’d recommend a pilot rather than a company-wide launch. First, we can reverse it if it fails, and a pilot would show us the effect on output and on customer cover. Second, waiting a few months costs us very little. I’d change my view if the early results showed customers waiting longer for answers.

contrast.q: A batch of our medicine may be contaminated. Should we recall it?
run: Undo it? A recall can be reversed. A harmed patient cannot.
Try it small? Not in time: the risk is now.
Cost of waiting? It grows with every hour.
So: decide now.
contrast.say: I’d recall it today. The harm cannot be undone, there is no time for a trial, and every day of delay adds risk. I’d review the decision as soon as the test results arrive.
contrast.note: The same words, “Should we…?”, and the lens points the other way. Seeing that is the skill.

talk: Think of a decision you made that you could not undo. How did you decide, and would you decide the same way today?
Which decisions in your work could be tried small first, and which could not?
When is waiting the right decision? Who tends to push for speed, and why?

lesson.title: Try It Small, or Do It Now

branches.asked: You are being asked to pick one thing over another, and to say why.
branches.breaks: When the options cannot be measured on one scale, a tidy table can hide the real disagreement.

leaves.name: Alphabet & BCG Matrix
leaves.desc: milk the cow, or risk it?

lens.g: Choose two or three criteria, and decide which comes first.

lens.q: How does each option do on those?
lens.g: One sentence per option. No spreadsheet.

lens.q: What do I give up with each?
lens.g: Every choice has a price. Name it.
That is the condition you can say out loud.

leads.w: A clear pick, with its price
leads.d: One option wins, and you say what it costs.
“A, unless…”, with the condition named.
The real answer is an option nobody has put forward.

example.q: Which supplier would you choose: the cheaper one or the reliable one?
run: What matters most: the cost of a late delivery, then price.
Cheaper: lower price, a patchy delivery record. Reliable: higher price, almost never late.
The price of choosing reliable: a few per cent more on every order.
What would flip it: the cheaper supplier’s record improving.
example.say: I’d choose the reliable supplier. A late delivery costs us more than the price difference, so I’m happy to pay a little extra for certainty. I’d reconsider if the cheaper supplier’s delivery record improved over the next year.

talk: Think of a recent choice between two good options. What mattered most, and did you say so out loud?
In your own field, what is the price of choosing the reliable option over the cheap one?
How do you decide when two people use different criteria for the same choice?

branches.asked: You are being asked where to start, when you cannot do everything at once.
branches.breaks: When everything really is urgent, or when people disagree about the ranking itself.

lens.q: What is urgent, and what is only loud?
lens.g: Urgent means a cost is arriving soon. Loud means someone is shouting.

lens.q: Which few things cause most of the trouble?
lens.g: Look for the vital few, not the long tail.
Some tasks unblock all the rest.

leads.d: Urgent, important, or blocking everything else.
Important, but not yet urgent.
Someone else can do it as well as you can.
Saying “not now” is part of the answer.

example.q: We have six open problems and one engineer. Where do we start?
run: Urgent: the payment errors, because orders are failing now.
The vital few: payments and the slow login together cause most of the complaints.
Dependencies: the other fixes cannot be tested until payments work.
Leave: the typos on the website.
example.say: I’d start with the payment errors, because they are stopping orders today and the other fixes depend on them. The slow login comes second, as it affects most users. The typos can wait, and I would tell people that clearly.

talk: What was loud in your work last week, and what was actually important?
Which one or two causes produce most of the trouble in your work? How do you know?
How do you tell a colleague “not now” without losing their trust?

lesson.title: Ninety Days and Thirteen Thousand Bricks

branches.asked: You are being asked to think ahead: what could happen, and are we ready?
branches.breaks: Numbers can give false comfort. The event that hurts is often the one nobody listed.

leaves.name: Novo Nordisk
leaves.desc: say the range, not the number

lens.g: The likely event and the severe one are often different.
Rough categories are enough: low, medium, high.
A sign you can actually watch for.
Prevent it, reduce it, prepare for it, or accept it knowingly.

leads.d: Stop the event from happening.
Make it smaller, or less damaging when it comes.
A warning sign and a plan B.
Low risk, high cost to avoid, and said out loud.

example.q: What happens to us if our main supplier fails in the winter?
run: Likelihood: low. Impact: severe, because production stops within two weeks.
Warning sign: two late deliveries in a row, or bad news about their finances.
Response: a second supplier for the critical part, and a buffer stock.
example.say: It’s unlikely but very serious, so I’d prepare rather than accept it. We would qualify a second supplier for the critical part and hold a buffer stock. The warning sign I’d watch for is two late deliveries in a row.

talk: What is the risk in your work that everyone knows about and nobody plans for?
Think of something that went wrong that nobody had listed. What does that tell you about lists of risks?
When is it right to accept a risk knowingly? Who should be told?

branches.asked: You are being asked to explain what went wrong — not to blame someone.
branches.breaks: There may be no single root cause. When causes interact, the search for one more “why” stops being useful.

lens.g: What, where, since when, how big. Say it as a fact, not a complaint.
Three or four possible causes: people, process, tools, outside events.

lens.q: What evidence would tell them apart?
lens.g: Start with the check that is cheapest.
Name your leading explanation and say how confident you are.

leads.w: A leading cause, with a confidence
leads.d: “Most likely X, because…”

leads.w: Two causes you cannot yet separate
leads.d: And the one check that would.
And exactly which data you need.

example.q: Why did customer complaints double in March?
run: The facts: complaints doubled from the first week of March, mostly about delivery.
Possible causes: the new delivery partner, a price change, a faulty batch.
Evidence: the rise began the week the partner changed. The price did not.
Cheapest check: split the complaints by delivery partner.
example.say: My leading explanation is the new delivery partner. The rise began the week we switched, and most of the complaints are about late delivery. I’m fairly sure but not certain, so the first thing I’d check is the complaints split by partner.

talk: Think of a problem you solved by finding its cause. What was your first explanation, and was it right?
When has blaming a person hidden the real cause?
How do you say “I’m fairly sure, but not certain” in your field?

branches.asked: You are being asked about what is fair or acceptable — and no tool can settle it for you.
branches.breaks: Here the thinking tools run out. Say what you would weigh, what you cannot resolve, and what would change your mind.

leaves.name: Medical Ethics (B2)
leaves.desc: where do we draw the line?

lens.q: Who is affected, and who decides?
lens.g: Name the people, not just “stakeholders”.

lens.q: Which principles pull against each other?
lens.g: Honesty and kindness. Fairness and loyalty. Say both.

lens.q: Would I accept this rule if it applied to me?
lens.g: The reversal test.
Facts you are missing are different from values you disagree about.

leads.d: “No, because…”
“Yes, unless…”
And say exactly what X is. Never a shrug.

example.q: Would it be fair to dismiss someone for a mistake the system allowed?
run: Affected: the employee, the team, the company. The company decides.
In tension: accountability and fairness.
Reversal: would I accept being dismissed if the system had let me make that mistake?
Not known: whether the weakness in the system was already known.
example.say: I’d say not, on its own. If the system allowed the mistake, the failure is shared, and dismissal would punish one person for a design problem. I’d change my view if the person had ignored a clear warning.

talk: Is there a rule in your profession that you would not accept if it applied to you?
When have honesty and kindness pulled in different directions at work? What did you do?
What is the difference between a fact you do not have and a value you disagree about? Give an example.

quiz.heading: Which kind of question is it?
quiz.lead: Eight questions you might be asked at work. Choose the branch each one belongs to, then check. Two of them are not what they first seem.

items.q: Why did customer complaints double in March?
items.why: Something has already happened and you are asked to explain it. That is a diagnosis.

items.q: Should we roll the new system out to every branch in January?
items.why: A commitment under uncertainty. The thinking is about reversibility, testing and the cost of waiting.

items.q: Is it acceptable to tell a patient only part of the truth?
items.why: It turns on what is fair and acceptable, and no tool settles it. You say what you weigh.

items.q: Should we fix the website or the payment system first?
items.why: It begins with “should we”, but the decision is already made. The question is order, so it belongs to priorities.

items.q: What happens to us if our main supplier fails in the winter?
items.why: You are asked to look ahead: how likely, how bad, and what is the plan.

items.q: Which of the two suppliers would you choose?
items.why: A choice between named options. Criteria and trade-offs are what the answer needs.

items.q: Would it be fair to dismiss someone for a mistake the system allowed?
items.why: It is about fairness and responsibility, not about facts you could look up.

items.q: We have six open problems and one engineer. Where do we start?
items.why: Too much to do and limited capacity. The answer is an order, with a reason for it.
